newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai rates seen remaining high near-term.
newsitem.headline: Thai rates seen remaining high near-term.

text.p: Thai interest rates are likely to remain high in the near-term despite the government's desire to see a significant decline to revive the sluggish economy, analysts said on Thursday.

"The rate outlook will depend on the economy. But based on the current situation any substantial drop in interest rates would be only wishful thinking," said Chao Kengchon of Thai Farmers Research, the research arm of Thai Farmers Bank.
"Although the money market is calmer now after weeks of turmoil, a number of risk factors remain and they will limit the Bank of Thailand's (manoeuvring) on its monetary policy," he said.
Analysts said money supply was likely to be squeezed by last week's government measures to bail out the property sector and bolster weakened financial institutions, keeping interest rates buoyed.
The central bank's resolve to fend off speculative activity in the weak baht, and the continued possibility of a U.S. rate hike, would also keep rates firm, they said.
Thai rates are among the highest in Asia. The minimum lending rate, at around 13.25 percent, has prompted borrowers to complain that it is too costly to borrow locally.

The Thai cabinet this week approved the issue of up to 100 billion baht of zero-coupon bonds to raise funds to rescue the cash-strapped property sector. About half of the amount is expected to be issued by April.
The bond issue would drain liquidity from the market and put upward pressure on interest rates, analysts said.

Nimit Nontapunthawat of Thailand's Bangkok Bank said the central bank's order last week that banks and finance firms set aside an additional 15 percent and 20 percent, respectively, in provisions for sub-standard assets, will also prevent rates from falling.
"The possibility that interest rates will increase is 90 percent. We now have to accept that the rate will not be reduced in the meantime," he said.

Rates could come down by a marginal 50-75 basis points if the gloomy economic picture changed and slow exports picked up later in the year, analysts said. Other factors which could help reduce interest rates were a narrowing in the current account deficit and easier money market liquidity, they said.
But all that was unlikely before the end of the second quarter, they said.

Some analysts argued that interest rates would have room to drop. With several new government pension and provident funds that would invest a portion of their 68 billion baht in capital later this year on the money market, liquidity would be boosted and rates would soften, they said.
